evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Q. alba and lists Texas in its native range at the state level.
US Forest Service describes the species as an eastern North American oak reaching Texas at the western edge of its range.
Texas vegetation/community sources place Q. alba in East Texas / West Gulf Coastal Plain forest communities rather than the project's Central/West Texas target zone.
No authoritative native record in three project target counties was located during B011 review.
target_zone_range.guardrail: The source-pool iNaturalist observation is not sufficient native-range evidence; Q. alba is commonly planted and oaks are frequently misidentified. A Texas-native state label does not satisfy the project's three-target-county rule.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for rounded lobes distributed along most of the blade plus pale gray flaky/scaly bark; unlike bur oak, there is no deep midleaf waist and no mossy-fringed acorn cup.
diagnostic_traits: leaves obovate to elliptic with typically 5–7 rounded lobes
sinuses often deep but distributed along much of blade rather than concentrated as a bur-oak waist
acorn cup shallow, often enclosing roughly one-quarter of nut

confusers.separator: Bur oak has huge leaves with deep middle sinuses and a strongly fringed cup; white oak has regular rounded lobes and a shallow non-fringed cup.
Post oak often has thick cruciform leaves with broad squared middle lobes and darker blockier bark; white oak usually shows a more evenly lobed blade.
Chinkapin oak has chestnut-like teeth rather than deep rounded lobes.

installation_guardrail: Do not install as a target-zone native; retain review evidence for comparison/reference.
